title: Cap. VIII Arg.: if God elects and reprobates without cause from men, he is acceptor of persons (Acts 10:34)
latin: Si Deus aliquos eligeret ab aeterno, aliquos reprobaret, absque causa se tenente ex parte hominum, tunc esset acceptor personarum. Videtur enim esse acceptor personarum, qui, duobus existentibus aequalibus, uni dat quod alteri denegat. Haec autem προσωπολημψία a Deo removetur, Actor. x. 34.
pass_a: If God from eternity were to elect certain ones, to reprobate certain ones, without a cause holding itself on the part of men, then he would be an acceptor of persons. For he seems to be an acceptor of persons, who, two existing equal, gives to one what he denies to the other. But this respect of persons is removed from God, Acts 10:34.
pass_b: Argument: if from eternity God elected some and reprobated others without a cause holding on the human side, then he would be an acceptor of persons. For he seems an acceptor of persons who, when two are equal, gives to one what he denies the other. But that respect of persons is removed from God (Acts 10:34).

lemmas.gloss: Acts 10:34 respect of persons removed from God
equal subjects, unequal gift = respect of persons

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: old Pelagian objection; Augustine Ep. 105 — same mass; debt to damned, unowed grace to freed
latin: Hanc fuisse veterem Pelagianorum objectionem passim apud Augustinum legimus. Epist. 105. Quod autem personarum acceptorem Deum se credere existimant, si credant quod sine ullis praecedentibus meritis cujus vult miseretur, et quos dignatur vocat, et quem vult religiosum facit, parum attendunt quod debita reddatur poena damnato, indebita gratia liberato, ut nec ille se indignum queratur, nec dignum se iste glorietur, atque ibi potius acceptionem nullam fieri personarum, ubi una eademque massa damnationis et offensionis involvit, ut liberatus de non liberatis discat, quod etiam sibi supplicium conveniret, nisi gratia subveniret. Eandem objectionem repellit Epist. 106. et contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. Huc igitur redit Augustini responsio, ut doceat non pertinere ad προσωπολημψία ubi quis de suo facit quod vult. Nam quamvis electo detur misericordia, reprobato tamen haud negatur justitia: Honoratur electus dono gratuito, non tamen fraudatur reprobatus beneficio sibi debito.
pass_a: That this was the old objection of the Pelagians we read everywhere in Augustine. Epistle 105. But that they think that they believe God to be an acceptor of persons, if they believe that without any preceding merits he has mercy on whom he will, and calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he will, they little attend that a due punishment is rendered to the damned, an unowed grace to the freed, so that neither that one complain himself unworthy, nor this one glory himself worthy, and that there rather no acceptance of persons is made, where one and the same mass of damnation and offense wraps, that the freed may learn from the not-freed that punishment would also have suited him, unless grace had come to help. The same objection he repels in Epistle 106 and Against two Letters of the Pelagians book 2 chapter 7. Hither therefore returns the response of Augustine, that he may teach that it does not pertain unto respect of persons where one does of his own what he wills. For although mercy is given to the elect, yet justice is by no means denied to the reprobate: The elect is honored with a gratuitous gift, yet the reprobate is not defrauded of a benefit owed him.
pass_b: This was the old Pelagian objection — we read it everywhere in Augustine. Epistle 105: those who think they make God an acceptor of persons if they believe that without preceding merits he has mercy on whom he will, calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he will, little notice that due punishment is rendered to the damned and unowed grace to the freed — so neither complains as unworthy, nor the other glories as worthy. Rather there is no respect of persons where one and the same mass of damnation and offense wraps all, that the freed may learn from the not-freed that punishment would have suited him too unless grace had helped. The same objection he repels in Epistle 106 and Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7. Augustine's answer comes to this: it is not respect of persons where one does of his own what he wills. Mercy is given the elect; justice is not denied the reprobate. The elect is honored with a gratuitous gift; the reprobate is not cheated of any benefit owed him.

lemmas.gloss: same mass; debt vs unowed grace
mercy to elect; justice not denied reprobate

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: Durandus, Thomas, Gerson — unequal gifts from liberality are not injustice
latin: Scholastici respondent magis succinte, Non esse injustum aut vitiosum dare inaequalia aequalibus, ubi aliquid datur ex mera liberalitate, sed ubi ex debito redditur. Sic Durandus lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. 2. resp. ad 1. In eandem sententiam Thomas, Non est iniquitas apud Deum, si inaequalia aequalibus praeparet. Hoc enim esset contra justitiae rationem, si praedestinationis effectus ex debito redderetur, et non daretur. Ex his enim quae ex gratia dantur, potest aliquis pro libito suo dare cui vult plus vel minus, dummodo nulli subtrahat debitum, Part. 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. resp. ad 3. Denique Gerson in Regulis Moralibus idem affirmat, Non est acceptio personarum nisi ubi debitum est et paritas utrobique, quia in gratis faciendis unum capere, alium dimittere, non est acceptio personarum. Ex hisce igitur perspicuum est, consequentiam Majoris in praedicto argumento fuisse plane nullam: quia in praedestinatione Deus non dat praedestinato debitam sed indebitam gratiam; atque similiter in reprobatione non denegat reprobato debitae sed indebitae gratiae beneficium.
pass_a: The Scholastics answer more succinctly, That it is not unjust or vicious to give unequals to equals, where something is given from mere liberality, but where it is rendered from debt. So Durandus book 1, distinction 41, question 2, response to 1. Unto the same sentence Thomas, There is no iniquity with God, if he prepare unequals for equals. For this would be against the reason of justice, if the effect of predestination were rendered from debt, and not given. For from those things which are given from grace, someone can at his pleasure give to whom he will more or less, provided he subtract from none what is owed, Part 1, question 23, article 5, response to 3. Finally Gerson in the Moral Rules affirms the same, There is not acceptance of persons except where there is debt and parity on both sides, because in making gratuitous things to take one, to dismiss another, is not acceptance of persons. From these therefore it is clear that the consequence of the Major in the foresaid argument was plainly null: because in predestination God gives not to the predestined an owed but an unowed grace; and likewise in reprobation he does not deny to the reprobate the benefit of an owed but of an unowed grace.
pass_b: The Scholastics answer more briefly: it is not unjust or vicious to give unequals to equals where the gift is from mere liberality — only where something is rendered from debt. So Durandus (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 2 ad 1). Thomas to the same effect: There is no iniquity with God if he prepare unequals for equals. It would be against justice if the effect of predestination were rendered as debt and not given. Of things given from grace, one may at pleasure give more or less to whom he will, provided he subtracts from none what is owed (ST I, q. 23 a. 5 ad 3). Gerson in the Moral Rules: there is no respect of persons except where debt and parity stand on both sides; in free gifts, to take one and dismiss another is not respect of persons. So the major's consequence in the argument is plainly null: in predestination God gives the predestined not owed but unowed grace; in reprobation he denies the reprobate not an owed benefit but an unowed one.

lemmas.gloss: predestination and reprobation concern unowed grace

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: Acts 10:34 concerns promised favor in every nation, not the eternal gratuitous decree
latin: Quod autem attinet ad illa Petri verba, Actor. x. 34, In veritate comperi quia non est personarum acceptor Deus, sed in omni gente qui timet eum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est ei, Spectant Dei favorem ex pacto et promisso jam quasi debitum, non aeternum illum et gratuitum favorem nullo pacto, nullo promissione obstrictum aut obligatum. Deus enim promittendo favorem suum timentibus se, ac sancte pieque viventibus, esset jam προσωπολημψία, si hominem pauperem aut ignobilem caste se colentem aspernaretur, divitem autem ac nobilem amplexaretur; aut si Judaeum religiosum favore suo prosequeretur, Gentilem vero juste, sobrie ac pie viventem negligeret. Hanc personarum acceptionem a Deo procul habendam docet Apostolus. At Deus nullo promisso aut pacto tenetur ad praedestinandum, vel non praedestinandum.
pass_a: But as to what pertains to those words of Peter, Acts 10:34, Of a truth I perceive that God is not an acceptor of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is accepted with him, They regard the favor of God from covenant and promise already as it were owed, not that eternal and gratuitous favor bound or obliged by no covenant, by no promise. For God, by promising his favor to those fearing him, and living holily and piously, would already be an acceptor of persons, if he were to spurn a poor or ignoble man chastely worshipping him, but to embrace a rich and noble one; or if he were to pursue a religious Jew with his favor, but to neglect a Gentile living justly, soberly, and piously. This acceptance of persons the Apostle teaches is to be held far from God. But God is held by no promise or covenant unto predestinating, or not predestinating.
pass_b: As for Peter's words (Acts 10:34) — Of a truth I perceive that God is not an acceptor of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is accepted with him — they regard God's favor from covenant and promise, already as it were owed, not that eternal gratuitous favor bound by no covenant or promise. For by promising favor to those who fear him and live holily and piously, God would already be an acceptor of persons if he spurned a poor or lowly man worshipping him chastely and embraced a rich noble, or if he favored a religious Jew and neglected a Gentile living justly, soberly, and piously. That respect of persons the Apostle teaches is far from God. But God is held by no promise or covenant to predestinate or not predestinate.

lemmas.gloss: Acts 10:34 = covenant favor, not eternal decree
no covenant binds God to elect or not

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: election and praeterition from mere good pleasure; those passed by were children of wrath
latin: Porro, in eligendo aut praetereundo non respicit aliquam externam circumstantiam gentis, nobilitatis, aut quid consimile, sed agit ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae. Denique, ii quos praeterit non possunt obtendere se Deum timuisse et juste vixisse, sed coguntur e contra agnoscere se fuisse irae filios, et minimo Dei beneficio indignissimos. Hic igitur locus Scripturae non probat, aut praedestinationem et reprobationem procedere ex causa aliqua se tenente ex parte hominum, aut Deum personarum acceptorem esse arguendum.
pass_a: Further, in electing or passing by he does not regard any external circumstance of nation, of nobility, or anything similar, but acts from the mere good pleasure of his will. Finally, those whom he passes by cannot pretend that they feared God and lived justly, but are compelled on the contrary to acknowledge that they were children of wrath, and most unworthy of the least benefit of God. This place of Scripture therefore does not prove either that predestination and reprobation proceed from some cause holding itself on the part of men, or that God is to be argued an acceptor of persons.
pass_b: Further: in electing or passing by he regards no external circumstance of nation, nobility, or the like, but acts from the mere good pleasure of his will. Finally, those he passes by cannot pretend they feared God and lived justly; they are compelled instead to acknowledge they were children of wrath, most unworthy of the least divine benefit. So this Scripture place proves neither that predestination and reprobation proceed from some cause holding on the human side, nor that God is to be charged as an acceptor of persons.

lemmas.gloss: electing/passing by from good pleasure alone
those passed by cannot claim just fear of God
